blocks.title: Listening Part 1
blocks.mode: Fresh classroom check: one play, no pausing, no support
blocks.instructions: Complete the form. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

stimulus.title: Recording IELTS-21-L1 transcript (teacher-private)
paragraphs: CLERK: Greenway Community Centre, bookings. How can I help?
DANIELA: Hello. I'd like to book a room for my daughter's eighteenth birthday party.
CLERK: Of course. What date were you thinking of?
DANIELA: Friday the twelfth of July, if possible.
CLERK: Let me check. I'm afraid Friday the twelfth is already taken. The day after is free, though.
DANIELA: The thirteenth? That's fine, actually. Let's say Saturday.
CLERK: And how many guests are you expecting?
DANIELA: We first said sixty, but we've cut the list, so around forty-five.
CLERK: In that case, the Main Hall would be too big. I'd suggest the Garden Room. It holds up to fifty and opens onto the garden.
DANIELA: That sounds lovely. What time could we have it from?
CLERK: What time would you like?
DANIELA: Guests will arrive at seven, but we'll need to decorate first, so could we have the room from half past five?
CLERK: Yes, that's fine. The Garden Room is thirty-two pounds an hour in the evening. During the day it's twenty-five.
DANIELA: OK. Is there a deposit?
CLERK: Yes, fifty pounds, which we return after the event if there's no damage.
DANIELA: Do you provide tables and chairs?
CLERK: Tables, chairs and a sound system are all included. You'll need to bring your own tablecloths, though.
DANIELA: And is there parking?
CLERK: There's no parking at the front, but you can use the car park behind the library, which is free after six.
CLERK: Could I take your name?
DANIELA: Daniela Moretti. That's M, O, R, E, T, T, I.
CLERK: Thank you. And on the day, please collect the keys from the café next door, because our office closes at five.

blocks.title: Reading Passage 1
blocks.mode: Fresh classroom check: twenty minutes, no dictionary, no support
blocks.instructions: Questions 11-14: which paragraph, A-F, contains the following information? Questions 15-19: write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Questions 20-23: choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

stimulus.title: The teenage clock
paragraphs: Parents have long complained that teenagers stay up late and find it hard to get up in the morning. This was often blamed on laziness or, more recently, on screens. Over recent decades, however, researchers who study sleep have offered a different explanation: much of the change is biological.

Everyone has an internal body clock that regulates when we feel sleepy and when we feel alert, partly through the hormone melatonin, which the body releases in the evening. During adolescence, the timing of this release shifts later, so that many teenagers do not feel sleepy until late in the evening. This shift appears in early adolescence and seems to reverse gradually in the early twenties. Teenagers' need for sleep, however, does not fall at the same rate; most teenagers still need more sleep than adults.

The result is a mismatch. If school begins early, a teenager who cannot fall asleep before eleven may regularly get far less sleep than they need. Researchers have linked such shortages to poorer concentration, lower mood and a greater risk of accidents among young drivers, although it is difficult to separate the effects of sleep from those of other factors in teenagers' lives. Weekend lie-ins, often criticised, may partly be an attempt to repay this 'sleep debt', although sleeping much later at weekends can make Monday mornings even harder.

Screens and social activities do play a part. Light from phones and computers in the evening may further delay sleepiness, and a busy social life can push bedtimes later. But these factors appear to add to the biological shift rather than cause it; the delay has been observed in many different cultures, including among teenagers with little access to technology.

In response, some schools have experimented with later start times. Reported results have often been encouraging: students sleep longer, attendance improves and fewer fall asleep in class. In some cases, schools also reported better exam results, but because other changes were often made at the same time, researchers are cautious about claiming that later starts alone were responsible. Nor are such changes simple to introduce. Bus timetables, after-school sports and the working hours of parents and teachers may all need to change, and some families find the new schedule inconvenient.

Sleep researchers generally agree that the solution is not simply to tell teenagers to go to bed earlier, since their bodies may not allow them to fall asleep. Instead, they recommend a combination of later school starts where possible, less screen use before bed, and more understanding from adults that teenage sleep patterns are not simply a matter of discipline.

items.prompt: a reference to a hormone involved in sleep
items.evidence: partly through the hormone melatonin
items.reason: Melatonin is named in paragraph B.

items.prompt: practical difficulties of changing school hours
items.evidence: Bus timetables, after-school sports and the working hours of parents and teachers may all need to change
items.reason: Practical obstacles to later starts.

items.prompt: evidence that late sleeping is not caused by technology alone
items.evidence: including among teenagers with little access to technology
items.reason: The delay exists even without much technology.

items.prompt: possible dangers of not getting enough sleep
items.evidence: a greater risk of accidents among young drivers
items.reason: 'Dangers' paraphrases 'risk of accidents'.

items.prompt: Teenagers generally need less sleep than adults.
items.evidence: most teenagers still need more sleep than adults
items.reason: The passage states the opposite.

items.prompt: The later timing of sleep continues throughout adult life.
items.evidence: seems to reverse gradually in the early twenties
items.reason: The shift reverses in early adulthood.

items.prompt: Evening light from screens may delay the feeling of sleepiness.
items.evidence: Light from phones and computers in the evening may further delay sleepiness
items.reason: Direct paraphrase.

items.prompt: Teenagers in rural areas sleep longer than those in cities.
items.evidence: Rural and urban teenagers are not compared.
items.reason: Different cultures are mentioned, but not rural versus urban.

items.prompt: Every family welcomes later school start times.
items.evidence: some families find the new schedule inconvenient
items.reason: 'Every family' is contradicted.

items.prompt: Why is it difficult to measure the effects of lost sleep, according to paragraph C?
options: A  Other factors in teenagers' lives also have effects.
B  Teenagers do not report their sleep accurately.
C  Researchers disagree about how much sleep is needed.
items.evidence: it is difficult to separate the effects of sleep from those of other factors
items.reason: B and C are not mentioned.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about weekend lie-ins?
options: A  They fully solve the problem of lost sleep.
B  They are a sign of laziness.
C  They may make the start of the week more difficult.
items.evidence: can make Monday mornings even harder
items.reason: They may 'partly' repay sleep debt (against A); the criticism is reported, not endorsed (against B).

items.prompt: Why are researchers cautious about reports of better exam results?
options: A  The results were never published.
B  Other changes were made at the same time.
C  Only a few students took part.
items.evidence: because other changes were often made at the same time
items.reason: The later start cannot be isolated as the cause.

items.prompt: What do sleep researchers recommend?
options: A  telling teenagers to go to bed earlier
C  a combination of measures, including later starts where possible
items.evidence: they recommend a combination of later school starts where possible
items.reason: A is rejected explicitly; B goes beyond 'less screen use'.

blocks.title: Plants in the office
blocks.instructions: Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

stimulus.title: Plants in the office
paragraphs: Many companies now place plants in offices, hoping to make workplaces more pleasant. Some studies have reported that employees in offices with plants say they feel more satisfied with their surroundings.

Claims that a few pot plants can significantly clean the air in a whole building, however, are treated with caution by many scientists, because laboratory tests in sealed chambers do not reflect conditions in a ventilated office.
Plants also need care. Without regular watering and enough light, they quickly look unhealthy, and a row of dying plants may do more harm than good to the atmosphere of an office.

items.evidence: employees in offices with plants say they feel more satisfied with their surroundings
items.reason: Direct paraphrase.

items.evidence: are treated with caution by many scientists
items.reason: Scientists are cautious, not in agreement with the claim.

items.prompt: Office plants are more expensive to maintain than air filters.
items.evidence: No cost comparison.
items.reason: Costs are not mentioned.

items.prompt: Poorly maintained plants may make an office feel worse.
items.evidence: may do more harm than good to the atmosphere of an office
items.reason: Direct paraphrase.
